hypothesis.rationale: Killing the front-end pod directly disrupts the entry point of the golden journey, causing immediate failures across all steps (home, catalogue, login, orders). This is a high-impact, common fault pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.

Killing the carts-db pod disrupts the data dependency for the carts service, which is part of the authenticated orders journey. This causes failures in the orders step (HTTP 201 expected) and potentially the login step if carts is used for session data. This is a common fault pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.

Killing the orders-db pod directly disrupts the data dependency for the orders service, which is critical for the authenticated orders step (HTTP 201 expected). This will cause the orders step to fail, and since orders-db is a backend dependency, it may also impact other services that rely on it. This is a common fault pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.

Killing the catalogue-db pod disrupts the data dependency for the catalogue service, which is part of the golden journey (catalogue step expects JSON array). This will cause the catalogue step to fail, and since catalogue-db is a backend dependency, it may also impact other services that rely on it. This is a common fault pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.

Killing the user-db pod disrupts the data dependency for the user service, which is used during the login step (HTTP 200 expected). This will cause the login step to fail, and since user-db is a backend dependency, it may also impact other services that rely on it. This is a common fault pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.

Killing the payment pod disrupts the payment service, which is a supporting service in the authenticated orders journey. Although the golden journey is read-only and may not directly invoke payment, payment is a dependency for order processing and its failure could cause cascading issues or timeouts. This tests resilience to supporting service failures, a common pattern (64.8% of PodChaos) with short duration to minimize recovery time.
